candidateRows: A historical resurrection case should distinguish agreed evidence from the disputed explanation and begin with four facts requiring explanation.
This move supplies the organizing framework for the entire affirmative case by defining both the evidentiary foundation and the explanatory question posed by the motion.
After introductory remarks about the debate and Ehrman's published position, Craig transitions into his affirmative framework and previews the four historical facts he will defend.
Jesus was buried in a tomb by Joseph of Arimathea, a conclusion supported by early independent sources and the improbability of Christian invention.
The burial claim establishes the identifiable tomb presupposed by the empty-tomb argument and forms one of the affirmative case's four foundational historical facts.
Craig begins his detailed evidentiary case with the burial, appealing to multiple early traditions and arguing that Joseph's role is unlikely to have been invented.
Jesus' tomb was found empty by women on the Sunday after the crucifixion, as supported by multiple traditions and an embarrassment consideration.
The empty tomb is one of the four principal facts the affirmative says every adequate hypothesis must explain and directly supports a bodily-resurrection inference.
Following the burial argument, Craig turns to the empty tomb and argues both that it has multiple attestation and that women witnesses would be an awkward invention.
Different individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus alive after his death, a fact supported by early testimony and multiple independent narratives.
Postmortem experiences constitute a principal evidentiary fact in the affirmative's cumulative explanation and must be accounted for by any competing hypothesis.
Craig moves from the empty tomb to reported appearances, emphasizing the early Pauline material, named recipients, group experiences, and independent narrative support.
The original disciples came sincerely to believe Jesus had risen despite Jewish expectations that strongly predisposed them against that conclusion.
The origin of resurrection belief is the fourth foundational fact and supplies the affirmative with a transformation that rival explanations must plausibly explain.
Craig argues that a crucified messianic claimant and prevailing beliefs about final resurrection made the disciples' new conviction unexpected and historically significant.
Resurrection best explains the four historical facts because it has broad explanatory virtues while proposed naturalistic alternatives lack comparable plausibility.
This is the affirmative's ultimate inference from the four facts to the proposition under debate and directly defends treating resurrection as the best explanation.
Ehrman's published position that historians cannot identify a miracle as the probable explanation of historical evidence.
After defending the factual foundation, Craig states his explanatory conclusion, contrasts it with naturalistic hypotheses, and challenges the methodological bar against miracles.
Historical conclusions concern degrees of probability and depend most strongly on contemporary, multiple, independent, consistent, and disinterested sources.
The move establishes the methodological standards Ehrman subsequently uses to challenge both the Gospel evidence and any historical conclusion of resurrection.
Following autobiographical remarks about his scholarly development, Ehrman defines historical inquiry as probabilistic and lays out criteria for reliable ancient evidence.
The Gospels are not sufficiently reliable historical accounts because they are late, non-eyewitness, orally transmitted, interested, and mutually inconsistent sources.
This move attacks the principal documentary basis for Craig's four facts and thereby weakens the evidentiary foundation from which the resurrection inference is drawn.
Craig's reliance on early and independent New Testament traditions to establish the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and disciples' belief.
Ehrman applies his historical criteria to the Gospels, tracing their stories through oral transmission and listing differences in passion and resurrection narratives.
Historical method cannot establish a resurrection miracle because history identifies what probably occurred while a miracle is definitionally the least probable occurrence.
This is the negative's governing reason that resurrection cannot be selected as a historical conclusion even if the underlying event might be accepted on theological faith.
Craig's claim that the resurrection may rationally be embraced as the historically best explanation despite its miraculous character.
After criticizing the sources, Ehrman argues that repeatable natural regularities ground probability whereas a miracle cannot satisfy the canons of historical inference.
Even an admittedly unlikely natural body-removal scenario remains historically more probable than resurrection because it invokes known human actions rather than a miracle.
The hypothetical operationalizes Ehrman's probability objection by presenting a natural alternative that need not be believed to rank above a miraculous explanation.
Craig's contention that no naturalistic alternative plausibly explains the empty tomb and resulting resurrection belief better than resurrection itself.
Ehrman proposes a deliberately unlikely removal-and-reburial account, argues that its component events remain naturally possible, and contrasts it with Craig's theological explanation.
A claim that God raised Jesus is theological rather than historical because historical inquiry cannot presuppose or investigate divine action.
This methodological distinction supplies Ehrman's central reason that historical evidence cannot establish the resurrection as a probable divine event.
Craig's contention that resurrection is the best historical explanation of the four cited facts.
After presenting a naturalistic alternative to the empty tomb, Ehrman argues that Craig's divine explanation exceeds the proper limits of historical research.
Ehrman's improbability objection ignores the evidential and alternative-hypothesis terms required to calculate the resurrection's conditional probability.
The probability analysis directly attacks the principal methodological objection offered against treating resurrection as the best explanation.
Ehrman's claim that a miracle cannot be historically probable because miracles are intrinsically the least probable occurrences.
Craig distinguishes background probability from explanatory power and argues that weak naturalistic alternatives can outweigh a low intrinsic probability.
Ehrman cannot coherently call divine resurrection improbable while also maintaining that historians can make no probability judgments about God.
The move challenges the internal consistency of Ehrman's methodological position rather than merely disputing a subsidiary historical fact.
Ehrman's combined claims that historians cannot assess God and that God's raising Jesus is historically improbable.
Craig distinguishes natural resurrection from the hypothesis that God raised Jesus and argues that assessing the latter requires assessing God's existence.
There is no contradiction in resurrection being unlikely on background knowledge alone yet highly probable when the specific evidence is included.
This distinction directly rebuts the alleged contradiction between a miracle's antecedent improbability and its proposed historical probability.
Ehrman's argument that historians would contradict themselves by finding the least probable kind of event most probable.
Craig separates two conditional probabilities and concludes that the evidentially conditioned probability may be high despite low antecedent probability.
Gospel imperfections do not defeat the four core facts because ancient sources need only be adequate and their central agreement remains historically strong.
The move defends the historical premises that the resurrection hypothesis is intended to explain, preserving the factual foundation of Craig's case.
Ehrman's source-quality wish list and his claim that Gospel discrepancies undermine the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and origin evidence.
Craig argues that ideal source standards are unrealistic, discrepancies concern details, and the Gospels agree on the central sequence of events.
Craig's appeals to scholarly authority are lopsided and do not establish his conclusions, which remain minority positions among historians.
The move contests Craig's attempt to support his factual case through asserted scholarly consensus and challenges the representativeness of that support.
Craig's repeated citation of modern scholars and claimed broad agreement concerning the four core historical facts.
Ehrman argues that agreement among theologically committed New Testament scholars is not proof and that Craig presents scholarly opinion selectively.
Paul does not attest Joseph's burial, and Craig inconsistently treats sparse early narratives as historical while discounting later embellishments.
The argument challenges both the early attestation of honorable burial and the consistency of Craig's method for evaluating ancient sources.
Craig's use of Pauline material and unembellished traditions to support Joseph of Arimathea's burial of Jesus.
Ehrman notes Paul's later date and silence about Joseph, proposes communal burial, and presses Craig on whether embellished later accounts are unhistorical.
The women and Joseph traditions could have been invented because they serve Mark's literary and theological purposes unusually well.
The move directly contests Craig's embarrassment-style inference for the empty tomb witnesses and the historicity of Joseph's burial role.
Craig's assertion that early Christians would not invent women as tomb witnesses or Joseph as Jesus' honorable burier.
Ehrman reads Mark as a theological proclamation centered on outsiders, making the women fit its agenda and Joseph a plausible invented follower.
Ancient postmortem appearances did not require a reanimated physical body, and divine resurrection remains a theological rather than historical inference.
The move attacks the inference from appearances to bodily resurrection and reiterates the central boundary Ehrman draws around historical conclusions.
Craig's inference that Pauline and disciple appearance traditions support an emptied tomb and a bodily resurrection caused by God.
Ehrman cites ancient visionary appearances and nonphysical bodies, then argues historians may report death or visions but not divine resurrection.
Paul's burial-and-raising formula implies an empty tomb within Jewish bodily-resurrection belief, while genuine appearances differ from subjective visions.
The move defends the link between early Pauline tradition, bodily resurrection, and the empty tomb while answering the visionary-appearance alternative.
Ehrman's charge that Craig inferred an empty tomb merely from appearances and ignored ancient nonphysical visionary experiences.
Craig says the burial-and-raising sequence implies transformed remains in Jewish thought and challenges Ehrman to distinguish resurrection appearances from visions.
Lack of direct access to God does not bar an inference to resurrection, since science and history routinely infer inaccessible explanatory entities from available evidence.
This directly defends the legitimacy of the inference at the center of Craig's case against the claim that historical method cannot reach a divine explanation.
Ehrman's position that historians cannot infer divine action because God is inaccessible to historical investigation.

Craig offers three connected answers: unobservable entities may be inferred, historians already infer an inaccessible past, and professional methodological limits do not settle what the evidence supports.
Treating divine resurrection as a historical explanation presupposes theistic belief and therefore cannot yield conclusions shared by historians across theological perspectives.
The move states Ehrman's central methodological reason why resurrection may be a theological conclusion but cannot qualify as a historical conclusion.
Craig's contention that historians or other investigators may legitimately infer that God raised Jesus from the dead.
Ehrman argues that historical inquiry must permit people with divergent religious commitments to assess common evidence and reach conclusions without first accepting belief in God.
Even if miracles occur, historians cannot demonstrate one as the best explanation because highly unlikely natural scenarios remain historically more accessible than supernatural action.
This supplies the comparative-explanation argument supporting Ehrman's methodological case and directly contests resurrection as the best historical explanation.
Craig's claim that probability reasoning and the four facts establish divine resurrection as the superior explanatory hypothesis.

Ehrman rejects the claim that he denies miracles in principle, then uses body-removal and mistaken-identity scenarios to argue that natural alternatives remain historically preferable despite being unlikely.
The four central facts remain historically established, natural alternatives fail to explain them adequately, and divine resurrection remains their best explanation.
This is Craig's consolidated defense of both premises of his overall case: the factual foundation and resurrection's comparative explanatory superiority.
Ehrman's challenges to the four facts, his natural alternative scenarios, and his claim that historians cannot infer divine causation.
Craig reaffirms the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and disciples' belief; answers objections about women and narrative differences; rejects body theft; and restates his methodological defense.
Craig has not established the four facts, and an ordinary body-removal scenario followed by visions remains more historically plausible than a divine resurrection.
The move attacks both the evidential premises and the claimed comparative superiority of resurrection, directly opposing the complete pro case.
Craig's concluding assertion that the four facts survived criticism and that family body removal plus visions is comparatively implausible.
Ehrman disputes the burial and empty tomb traditions, interprets appearances as visions, questions evidence about disciples' martyrdom, and answers Craig's objections to a family-removal hypothesis.
Resurrection belief can be explained as a developing interpretation of Jesus' death in light of scripture, followed by exaltation belief, visions, circulating stories, and later Gospel narratives.
This provides Ehrman's affirmative historical alternative for the origins of resurrection belief rather than relying only on methodological exclusion of miracles.
Craig's claim that only an actual resurrection adequately explains the disciples' belief, reported appearances, and subsequent traditions.

Ehrman proposes that followers reread suffering-and-vindication scriptures, concluded Jesus had been exalted, developed expectations of his return, experienced or reported visions, and eventually produced resurrection narratives.
Historical work requires shared and observable evidential assumptions across theological perspectives, so appeals to unobservable divine activity are not valid historical criteria.
The answer clarifies the methodological standard underlying Ehrman's entire opposition to treating resurrection as a demonstrable historical event.
The questioner's challenge that justified metaphysical beliefs about God need not fall outside interdisciplinary historical reasoning.
Ehrman allows that historians disclose and defend presuppositions but insists their operative standards must be shared across theological positions and rooted in publicly observable evidence.
Requiring methodological atheism is self-defeating because agnosticism about God cannot support a judgment that resurrection is improbable relative to natural alternatives.
The reply targets the logical coherence of Ehrman's central methodological restriction and defends making a resurrection inference from historical evidence.
Ehrman's requirement that valid historical explanations rest on shared observable assumptions and exclude appeals to divine activity.

Craig argues that if historians cannot judge divine action, they also cannot assign it low probability or compare it unfavorably with naturalistic accounts, while philosophers remain free to infer it.

Historical evidence cannot select Craig's preferred divine explanation over rival theological stories, because both are theological interpretations evaluated by theological rather than historical criteria.
The theological-underdetermination argument directly challenges the claim that the historical facts uniquely or preferentially identify the Christian resurrection explanation.
Craig's recurring claim that the four historical facts support the specific conclusion that the God of Israel raised Jesus.
Ehrman accepts theology as a mode of knowledge but constructs a rival supernatural account to show that historical facts alone cannot privilege Craig's specific theological interpretation.
Rival theological hypotheses can be comparatively evaluated, and the resurrection is more plausible and less ad hoc when interpreted within Jesus' religious-historical context.
This answers the underdetermination challenge by supplying the contextual and comparative basis for preferring Craig's specific resurrection hypothesis.
Ehrman's argument that an invented supernatural explanation is historically no less likely than the claim that Israel's God raised Jesus.

Craig calls the rival account ad hoc, invokes Jesus' claims and Israelite context as interpretive evidence, and maintains that theological hypotheses can be assessed philosophically by explanatory criteria.
Craig does not base his resurrection case on assigning a numerical probability, because the probability of a free divine agent acting is inscrutable.
This distinction directly answers the numerical-probability objection and prevents Craig's historical case from depending on a quantified prior probability for divine action.
Ehrman's argument that a resurrection is historically unacceptable because miracles are intrinsically too improbable.
Following a request for the numbers behind Craig's probability equation, Craig cites Swinburne's calculation but says his own argument does not assign such numbers.
The resurrection should be compared with naturalistic alternatives through inference to the best explanation rather than excluded by methodological atheism.
This states Craig's governing method for deciding the motion and argues that resurrection outperforms rival explanations unless supernatural agency is excluded in advance.
Ehrman's claim that historical method cannot admit a miraculous resurrection as the most probable explanation.
Craig replaces numerical calculation with standard explanatory criteria and argues that Ehrman has supplied no basis for treating God or divine resurrection as improbable.
Statistical models cannot demonstrate either God's existence or Jesus' resurrection and function chiefly to persuade people already inclined to believe.
The move attacks the legitimacy and persuasive force of probabilistic apologetics at the methodological level rather than disputing only a particular numerical input.
Craig's appeal to probability theory and Swinburne's calculation while defending the rational assessment of resurrection.
Ehrman dismisses the discussion of statistical probabilities for resurrection and God as academically unserious and incapable of establishing supernatural reality.
Repeated reports of miracles do not increase their historical probability because every reported instance must be evaluated separately and remains improbable.
The claim supplies a general rule for handling accumulated miracle reports and blocks recurrence alone from overcoming Ehrman's historical improbability objection.
The suggestion that recurrence of reported miracles over time may raise the probability that a miracle occurred.
In answering a question about recurring miracle reports, Ehrman says recurrence does not make miracles probable because each alleged event requires its own evaluation.
Accepting Jesus' miracles while rejecting comparable ancient miracle workers reflects religious tradition rather than a consistently applied historical standard.
The comparison challenges the claimed uniqueness and explanatory privilege of Jesus' resurrection by alleging that confessional commitments determine which miracle reports receive credit.
Craig's contention that Jesus' resurrection is plausible within its religious-historical context and superior to ad hoc alternatives.
Ehrman invokes Muhammad, Apollonius, and numerous ancient wonder workers to argue that Christians discount analogous traditions while privileging their own inherited claims.
Miracle claims are rejected or accepted according to their historical evidence, and the evidence for Jesus as a miracle worker is stronger than the late reports about Muhammad or Apollonius.
This rebuttal denies that confessional bias explains the differential treatment of miracle traditions and restores comparative evidential support for the case concerning Jesus.
Ehrman's argument that Christians privilege Jesus while dismissing comparable miracle reports solely because of religious tradition.
Craig says he is open to miracles outside Christianity but argues that Muhammad's reports are late, Apollonius traditions are legendary, and Jesus' miracle ministry is broadly historically accepted.
